title: The cowherd's skills
hook: eleven skills of a good cowherd, and of a good monk

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Gosinga grove, and your line, each lights it differently. Did you notice someone whose light isn't yours? Day four hundred twenty-nine.

Ask a farmer what makes a good herder, and you won't hear about love of animals or a sense of calling. You'll hear about flies. Wounds. Which field still has grass in August. Whether you know your own cows by sight. Farming is a craft of small, boring, crucial skills. The Buddha grew up in farming country, and once he listed eleven of those skills, one by one, and then showed that each was also a skill of the spiritual life. Today: the cowherd's skills.
screen: `ASK A FARMER: NOT LOVE, BUT FLIES.` → `SMALL, BORING, CRUCIAL SKILLS.` → `ELEVEN OF THEM, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-third discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the greater discourse on the cowherd. A good cowherd knows the shape of his cattle and knows their markings. He picks the flies' eggs out of their hides. He dresses their wounds. He makes smoke to drive the insects off. He knows the watering place, and knows when they've had enough to drink. He knows the road, and he knows good pasture. He doesn't milk them dry, but leaves some for the calves. And he gives special care to the old bulls who lead the herd. Now the Buddha turns each one. Knowing the shape of the cattle is knowing the body: what it's made of. Knowing the markings is knowing that a fool and a wise person are marked by what they do. Picking out the flies' eggs is not letting thoughts of greed, ill will and cruelty settle in and hatch. Dressing the wounds is guarding the senses. Making smoke is teaching others what you've learned. The watering place is going to people who know more, and asking questions. Knowing when they've drunk is feeling the meaning land. The road is the eightfold path. The pasture is the four foundations of mindfulness. Not milking dry is accepting only what you need from people who give. And honoring the old bulls is kindness toward elders, in deed, word and thought. Notice how unglamorous these are. Not one is a vision or a miracle. Flies' eggs. Smoke. The spiritual life, here, is a craft, and crafts are learned one small skill at a time.
screen: `ELEVEN SKILLS OF A GOOD COWHERD` · `FLIES' EGGS: THOUGHTS THAT HATCH` · `THE PASTURE: THE FOUR MINDFULNESSES` · `A CRAFT, LEARNED SKILL BY SKILL` · then, large: `KNOW YOUR HERD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one small skill. Today, take the flies' eggs. Sit, and watch the mind. When a sour thought lands, irritation, envy, a little cruelty, don't fight it and don't feed it. Notice it, the way a cowherd spots an egg on a hide, and gently brush it off by coming back to the breath. Do it again when the next one lands. That's the whole skill. The bell holds the time.
The cowherd's skills. Eleven plain crafts of tending a herd, each one a craft of tending a mind. Today's word.
Your line: know your herd. Today, pick one of the eleven, maybe the smoke, the watering place or the old bulls, and practice it once on purpose. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often draw on farming and herding similes like MN 33 to present practice as a set of learnable skills: restraint of the senses, removing harmful thoughts, asking those more learned, moderation in what one accepts, and respect for elders.

myth: a good cowherd takes every drop of milk
he doesn't milk dry; he leaves some, as a monk accepts only what he needs from those who give.
the road, in the simile, is the eightfold path
and the pasture is the four foundations of mindfulness.
most of the eleven skills are about visions and miracles
they're plain crafts: flies' eggs, smoke, wounds, water and pasture.

fork.setup: you're a cowherd. you spot flies' eggs on a cow's hide. it's late, and you're tired. what does a good cowherd do?
options: pick them out now, before they hatch.
fork.reveal: a good cowherd picks the eggs out. the Buddha's monk does the same with thoughts of greed, ill will and cruelty, before they settle in.

original.note: Pali gopalaka: cowherd (go, cow + palaka, keeper). the discourse is the Mahagopalaka Sutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: spiritual life is about big moments of insight.
what it means: it's a craft, built from small daily skills like a herder's.

what a scholar hears: the very next discourse, MN 34, keeps the herder: a foolish cowherd drives his cattle across the Ganges where there is no ford, and a wise one crosses at the ford, strongest bulls first.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 33, Mahagopalaka Sutta (the greater discourse on the cowherd)

notes: MN 33 paraphrased; the eleven factors are given positively (the sutta first lists them as failures). Confirm each match between the cowherd's skill and the monk's.
'The Buddha grew up in farming country' is a general statement about the Sakyan region; confirm or soften.
Trapdoor summarizes MN 34 (Culagopalaka): the Magadhan cowherds at the Ganges; confirm.
